claims.text: The report is a summary of a classified one and answers a statute: 'This report is an unclassified summary of a classified report that we sent to you on April 1, 1988.' The review 'is in response to section 1133 of Public Law 100-180, which requires that the Comptroller General report to the defense committees on this subject.'

GAO's central finding: 'We found that the Department of Defense does not adequately follow criteria to be used in determining the need to establish programs as special accessrequired. The definition of special accessprograms is not clear within the Department of Defense and, until recently, the oversight role of the Office of the Secretary of Defense in the programs' creation has been limited.'

Nobody held a list: 'The Deputy Under Secretary of Defense for Policy is required to maintain a listing of all special access programs, but does not do so because of security concerns.' GAO adds that 'the Secretary's Office has no centralized office with cognizance of all special access programs'.

The Army reform is dated to 1983-84, not 1994: 'A DOD review of Army special access programs in 1983 revealed systemic weaknesses in various management areas, which resulted in establishment of a central oversight office in September 1984.'
Creation authority is held by four people: 'Only the three service secretaries and Deputy Under Secretary of Defense for Policy are authorized to establish special access programs.'

dossier.narrative: The board's oversight case has always turned on a simple claim: that the special access system is not policed by the department that runs it. This report is Congress's own auditor saying so in 1988, in an unclassified summary of a classified report, to Les Aspin, Bill Chappell Jr., Sam Nunn and John C. Stennis. Three findings carry. First, creation authority is narrow and named: only the three service secretaries and the Deputy Under Secretary of Defense for Policy may establish a special access programme. Second, nobody held the list: the Deputy Under Secretary for Policy was required to maintain a listing of all special access programmes and did not, on security grounds, and the Secretary's office had no centralized office with cognizance of all of them. Third, and this is the finding that moves two existing nodes, the reform chain starts earlier than the board had it: a DoD review of Army special access programs in 1983 revealed systemic weaknesses which resulted in the establishment of a central oversight office in September 1984. The January 1994 dates on dod-sap-reform-1994 and sapoc stand; what changes is that they are no longer the beginning.
